children: Crude oil futures closed mixed on Monday following attacks by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis on a ‌Yemeni military training camp and renewed attacks on Saudi energy, airport, and military facilities.

for December fell 0.5% to $98.54/bbl, while the WTI November contract, which expires Tuesday, jumped 2.2% to $103.66/bbl on thin volume.
The Houthis said they carried out attacks on ​a Saudi Aramco (
) facility in Yanbu on the Red Sea coast, the Shaybah oilfield, King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, and Abha airport; ​Saudi authorities have not confirmed the claims.
Separately, an oil tanker caught fire and exploded after striking a mine in the southern Strait of Hormuz on Sunday, according to Iranian media.

Crude flows through the Middle East fell to a seven-day average of ~8.5M bbl/day last week, down from more than 20M bbl/day the previous week, analytics firm Kpler said, due to the ​increased threats to commercial shipping.
U.S. petroleum product futures have mostly gained in recent days despite President Trump's
on Russian energy exports, aiming to increase supply of crude and products, particularly diesel, on global markets.
Trump's waiver and the release of Russian diesel puts "a few more barrels back on a market that has been running on fumes," Price Futures Group senior market analyst Phil Flynn said in a note.

However, "these volumes are small compared with the global shortfall, Russian refining capacity is still damaged, both sides continue to target energy infrastructure, and inventories - especially U.S. distillates - remain historically low," Flynn wrote.
